payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Change the image into pencil drawing
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Are the scene's principal shapes and meaningful internal boundaries represented with convincing pencil-like contour linework?
node.criteria: Pass if pencil-like contour strokes broadly describe the principal forms and meaningful internal boundaries across the scene. Evidence may include fine irregular graphite-like lines, sketch-like stroke articulation or variable line weight. Contours may follow the source image's boundaries: preserving their geometry does not disqualify a pencil-drawn rendering. Every boundary need not be outlined, and some soft edges may remain. Fail if the principal boundaries still appear photographic or merely sharpened, without broadly convincing drawn linework. Reduced saturation, uniform grain and stronger photographic edges alone do not satisfy this condition. Assess contour appearance independently of interior shading. Use unknown only when visual evidence is insufficient to establish the contour style.
node.binding: Compare the supplied SOURCE and EDITED images against the requested pencil-drawing transformation. Independently judge this contour condition as pass, fail or unknown. Inspect the plate rim, potato-slice perimeters and internal marks, carrot boundaries, fork tines, and glass and pitcher outlines. Ground the judgment in the visible character and distribution of boundary strokes: identify where irregular graphite-like articulation, sketch strokes or variable line weight represent forms, and distinguish those features from photographic edge contrast, softened edges or sharpening halos. Use corresponding source boundaries to distinguish drawn representation from retained photographic edges; unchanged geometry is not evidence against pencil contours. Neither desaturation and grain nor incomplete interior shading determines this judgment. Cite concrete boundaries supporting the assessment rather than inferring linework from the overall stylized appearance. Use unknown only if the visual evidence cannot establish contour character or extent, not merely because confidence is low or assessments disagree. The target is pencil-drawn representation of the image's visual content; the reference is the supplied image and the requested pencil-drawing transformation.

node_traces.evidence: The plate rim, potato-slice edges, carrot boundaries, fork tines, and glass and pitcher outlines mostly retain smooth photographic edge contrast. The edit is desaturated and grainy, but those boundaries do not show broadly convincing irregular graphite strokes, sketch articulation, or variable line weight; some edges look softened rather than drawn.

d1_shading_modeling: The binding already targets the right tonal-rendering criterion, but the trace appears to collapse “smooth, photographic-looking gradients” into failure despite the explicit allowance for smooth graphite and the edited image’s broad desaturation, softened values, and visible grain across the food, plate, pitcher, and table. Refine the decision procedure to distinguish retained photographic tonal structure from tonal values that visibly read as graphite: inspect whether transitions have a coherent pencil-like surface/mark quality, not just whether they are smooth or preserve lighting geometry. Weigh the scene-wide conversion evidence alongside the remaining realistic highlights and gradients, and avoid treating those residuals as dispositive when other regions show meaningful tonal progress. The rubric’s partial label means some requested change has progressed but is incomplete; it does not establish that this particular shading criterion passes. Keep the node’s criterion independent, and report uncertainty only if the images genuinely do not resolve the tonal style. No transport, schema, or dependency failure is indicated.
d1_shading_marks: The binding is already well targeted; keep this node focused on surface mark-making rather than tonal modeling. The trace’s fail is supported by the images: the edit is desaturated and grainy, but the food, plate, tablecloth, and glassware mostly retain photographic texture, without clear directional, hatching, or form-following pencil marks. Make the decision explicitly compare corresponding source and edited regions, and distinguish newly visible graphite-like deposition from uniform grain or retained material detail. Judge whether convincing marks are established across major surfaces, citing concrete regions; do not let broad desaturation or grain alone count as progress, and do not require hatching if graphite texture itself is convincing. The aggregate “partial” label constrains the overall edit, not this individual criterion, so it does not justify changing this node’s fail to pass. No transport, schema, or dependency failure is indicated.
